claim: The human TP53 gene expresses at least twelve p53 isoforms through alternative splicing of intron-2 (Δ40) and intron-9 (α, β, γ), initiation of transcription in intron-4 (Δ133) and alternative initiation of translation at codon 40 (Δ40) and codon 160 (Δ160).
source: We previously reported that the human TP53 gene expresses at least twelve p53 isoforms through alternative splicing of intron-2 (Δ40) and intron-9 (α, β, γ), initiation of transcription in intron-4 (Δ133) and alternative initiation of translation at codon 40 (Δ40) and codon 160 (Δ160).
evidence: This is a statement about the structure and expression of the TP53 gene, referencing previous work by the authors.

claim: p53 isoforms regulate cell cycle progression, programmed cell death, replicative senescence, viral replication, cell differentiation and angiogenesis.
source: All animal models (zebrafish, drosophila and mouse) of p53 isoforms and experimental data in human cells of diverse tissue origins have consistently shown that p53 isoforms regulate cell cycle progression, programmed cell death, replicative senescence, viral replication, cell differentiation and angiogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to animal models and experimental data across multiple species and tissue types.

claim: Abnormal expressions of p53 isoforms are found in a wide range of human cancers including breast and colon cancers.
source: Several clinical studies reported that abnormal expressions of p53 isoforms are found in a wide range of human cancers including breast and colon cancers and that p53 isoforms are associated with cancer prognosis (Joruiz and Bourdon, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical studies.

claim: p53 isoforms are associated with cancer prognosis.
source: Several clinical studies reported that abnormal expressions of p53 isoforms are found in a wide range of human cancers including breast and colon cancers and that p53 isoforms are associated with cancer prognosis (Joruiz and Bourdon, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical studies.

claim: Δ133p53β promotes cancer stem cell potential and metastasis formation in a xenograft mouse model.
source: Recently, we reported that Δ133p53β promotes cancer stem cell potential and metastasis formation in a xenograft mouse model (Arsic et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: WT TAp53α protein plays a pre-eminent role in preventing human cancer formation and progression to metastasis.
source: Compelling evidence indicates that WT TAp53α protein, plays a pre-eminent role in preventing human cancer formation and progression to metastasis.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about p53 function.

claim: WT TAp53α protein prevents cell migration and invasion which are the main traits of Epithelial to Mesenchymal Transition (EMT).
source: In particular, WT TAp53α protein prevents cell migration and invasion which are the main traits of Epithelial to Mesenchymal Transition (EMT), which itself involves global genome reprogramming that drives cancer progression to metastasis (McDonald et al., 2011; Suva et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Most TAp53α missense mutant proteins promote EMT, inducing cancer cells to leave their primary tumor site and disseminate, leading to metastasis.
source: Conversely, most TAp53α missense mutant proteins promote EMT, inducing cancer cells to leave their primary tumor site and disseminate, leading to metastasis (Bernard et al., 2013; Gadea et al., 2007; Muller et al., 2009; Roger et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Δ133p53α mRNA was detected in 97/273 (35.5%) of the breast tumors analyzed.
source: Expression of Δ133p53α mRNA was detected in 97/273 (35.5%), Δ133p53β mRNA in 23/273 (8.4%) and Δ133p53γ mRNA in 56/221 (25.3%) of the breast tumors analyzed (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the RT-PCR analysis of breast tumor samples.

claim: Δ133p53β mRNA was detected in 23/273 (8.4%) of the breast tumors analyzed.
source: Expression of Δ133p53α mRNA was detected in 97/273 (35.5%), Δ133p53β mRNA in 23/273 (8.4%) and Δ133p53γ mRNA in 56/221 (25.3%) of the breast tumors analyzed (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the RT-PCR analysis of breast tumor samples.

claim: Δ133p53γ mRNA was detected in 56/221 (25.3%) of the breast tumors analyzed.
source: Expression of Δ133p53α mRNA was detected in 97/273 (35.5%), Δ133p53β mRNA in 23/273 (8.4%) and Δ133p53γ mRNA in 56/221 (25.3%) of the breast tumors analyzed (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the RT-PCR analysis of breast tumor samples.

claim: Samples identified as expressing Δ133p53β mRNA also express Δ133p53β at the protein level.
source: Samples identified as expressing Δ133p53β mRNA also express Δ133p53β at the protein level, confirming the RT-PCR analysis data and that Δ133p53β protein is expressed in tumor samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Δ133p53β or Δ133p53γ are tightly associated with Δ133p53α expression [21/23 (91.3%); 53/56 (94.6%), respectively].
source: Δ133p53β or Δ133p53γ are tightly associated with Δ133p53α expression [21/23 (91.3%); 53/56 (94.6%), respectively].
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the expression data from breast tumors.

claim: Only 25% of tumors expressing Δ133p53γ also express Δ133p53β (14/56).
source: However, only 25% of tumors expressing Δ133p53γ also express Δ133p53β (14/56, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 3.

claim: Δ133p53β was significantly less frequently expressed in HER2 positive and luminal/HER2+ tumors than in other breast cancer subtypes.
source: However, Δ133p53β was significantly less frequently expressed in HER2 positive and luminal/HER2+ tumors than in other breast cancer subtypes (2/69, Fisher's exact test, p≤0.042, Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test) and presented in Figure 1C.

claim: TP53 mutations were identified in 64 tumors (64/260, 24.6%).
source: TP53 mutations were identified in 64 tumors (64/260, 24.6%).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutation analysis data from the tumor cohort.

claim: Δ133p53β expression was significantly associated with TP53 mutation status (χ2 = 5.625, p≤0.018).
source: Δ133p53β expression was significantly associated with TP53 mutation status (χ2 = 5.625, p≤0.018, Figure 1C), whereas Δ133p53α and Δ133p53γ expression levels were not (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by chi-square statistical analysis and presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Δ133p53α and Δ133p53γ expression levels were not associated with TP53 mutation status.
source: Δ133p53β expression was significantly associated with TP53 mutation status (χ2 = 5.625, p≤0.018, Figure 1C), whereas Δ133p53α and Δ133p53γ expression levels were not (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: In all tumors, Δ133p53α, Δ133p53β or Δ133p53γ carried the same TP53 gene mutation.
source: In all tumors, Δ133p53α, Δ133p53β or Δ133p53γ carried the same TP53 gene mutation, indicating that all the corresponding mRNAs derive from cancer cells and not from normal stromal or inflammatory cells.
evidence: This claim is based on mutation analysis data and leads to an inference about the cellular origin of the isoforms.

claim: Δ133p53β was associated with cancer progression (CP: χ2 = 5.953, p≤0.015) and death (χ2 = 7.126, p≤0.008).
source: Δ133p53β was associated with cancer progression (CP) and death (CP: χ2 = 5.953, p≤0.015, death: χ2 = 7.126, p≤0.008) (Figure 1C), while Δ133p53α and Δ133p53γ were not.
evidence: This claim is supported by univariate statistical analysis and presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Δ133p53α and Δ133p53γ were not associated with cancer progression and death.
source: Δ133p53β was associated with cancer progression (CP) and death (CP: χ2 = 5.953, p≤0.015, death: χ2 = 7.126, p≤0.008) (Figure 1C), while Δ133p53α and Δ133p53γ were not.
evidence: This claim is supported by univariate statistical analysis.

claim: Δ133p53β expression was associated with cancer progression in WT TP53 breast cancer patients (Kaplan-Meier log-rank test, CP: χ2 = 5.232, p≤0.022).
source: Importantly, Δ133p53β expression was also associated with cancer progression in WT TP53 breast cancer patients (Kaplan-Meier log-rank test, CP: χ2 = 5.232, p≤0.022) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), indicating that the association between ∆133p53β expression and cancer progression is not due to TP53 mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier log-rank statistical analysis and presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The association between ∆133p53β expression and cancer progression is not due to TP53 mutation.
source: Importantly, Δ133p53β expression was also associated with cancer progression in WT TP53 breast cancer patients (Kaplan-Meier log-rank test, CP: χ2 = 5.232, p≤0.022) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), indicating that the association between ∆133p53β expression and cancer progression is not due to TP53 mutation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Δ133p53β is associated with cancer progression even in WT TP53 patients.

claim: The luminal-A subtype was the most significant independent predictor of disease-free survival (HR = 3.09, 95% CI, 1.78 to 5.38, p<1.10–4).
source: We observed that the luminal-A subtype was, as expected, the most significant independent predictor of disease-free survival (HR = 3.09, 95% CI, 1.78 to 5.38, p<1.10–4) and overall survival (HR = 4.15, 95% CI, 2 to 8.62, p<1.6 10–4, Table 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate Cox's regression analysis presented in Table 5A.

claim: The luminal-A subtype was the most significant independent predictor of overall survival (HR = 4.15, 95% CI, 2 to 8.62, p<1.6 10–4).
source: We observed that the luminal-A subtype was, as expected, the most significant independent predictor of disease-free survival (HR = 3.09, 95% CI, 1.78 to 5.38, p<1.10–4) and overall survival (HR = 4.15, 95% CI, 2 to 8.62, p<1.6 10–4, Table 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate Cox's regression analysis presented in Table 5A.

claim: Δ133p53β stood out as the most significant independent predictor of cancer recurrence within the luminal-A subgroup (Hazard ratio [HR], 7.93; 95% CI, 2.52 to 25; p<4.31 10–4).
source: Among all the parameters included in the analysis (Δ133p53β, TP53 mutation, tumor grade, lymph node metastasis and tumor size [>20 mm]), Δ133p53β stood out as the most significant independent predictor of cancer recurrence and death within the luminal-A subgroup regardless of TP53 mutation status or presence of lymph node metastasis (Hazard ratio [HR], 7.93; 95% CI, 2.52 to 25; p<4.31 10–4; [HR], 3.29; 95% CI, 1.125 to 9.63; p<0.03, Table 5B, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate Cox's regression analysis presented in Table 5B.

claim: Δ133p53β stood out as the most significant independent predictor of death within the luminal-A subgroup ([HR], 3.29; 95% CI, 1.125 to 9.63; p<0.03).
source: Among all the parameters included in the analysis (Δ133p53β, TP53 mutation, tumor grade, lymph node metastasis and tumor size [>20 mm]), Δ133p53β stood out as the most significant independent predictor of cancer recurrence and death within the luminal-A subgroup regardless of TP53 mutation status or presence of lymph node metastasis (Hazard ratio [HR], 7.93; 95% CI, 2.52 to 25; p<4.31 10–4; [HR], 3.29; 95% CI, 1.125 to 9.63; p<0.03, Table 5B, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate Cox's regression analysis presented in Table 5B.

claim: Δ133p53β in luminal-A breast cancer enhances on average by 8 times the risk of recurrence and by 3 times the risk of death.
source: Thus, Δ133p53β in luminal-A breast cancer, which predominantly expresses WT TP53, enhances on average by 8 times the risk of recurrence and by 3 times the risk of death in an otherwise excellent prognostic group.
evidence: This claim is based on the hazard ratios calculated from the multivariate Cox's regression analysis.

claim: WT TP53 gene can be associated with cancer recurrence and death if it expresses Δ133p53β.
source: This indicates that WT TP53 gene can be associated with cancer recurrence and death if it expresses Δ133p53β.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clinical data showing Δ133p53β association with poor outcomes in luminal-A breast cancer, which predominantly expresses WT TP53.

claim: MCF7 cells were very weakly invasive.
source: As expected, MCF7 cells were very weakly invasive and MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells showed a significantly higher invasiveness as compared to parental MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells showed a significantly higher invasiveness as compared to parental MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: As expected, MCF7 cells were very weakly invasive and MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells showed a significantly higher invasiveness as compared to parental MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The two MDA-MB-231 cell lines expressed similar levels of TAp53 and alpha TP53 mRNA variants.
source: We found that whereas the two cell lines expressed similar levels of TAp53 and alpha TP53 mRNA variants, the more invasive MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN expressed higher levels of Δ133p53, beta and gamma mRNA variants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The more invasive MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN expressed higher levels of Δ133p53, beta and gamma mRNA variants.
source: We found that whereas the two cell lines expressed similar levels of TAp53 and alpha TP53 mRNA variants, the more invasive MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN expressed higher levels of Δ133p53, beta and gamma mRNA variants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: TAp53α protein expression is similar between MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN.
source: In agreement with the RT-qPCR data, TAp53α protein expression is similar between MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN, while all the other p53 protein isoforms, notably ∆133p53β are expressed at higher levels in MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: All the other p53 protein isoforms, notably ∆133p53β are expressed at higher levels in MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN.
source: In agreement with the RT-qPCR data, TAp53α protein expression is similar between MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN, while all the other p53 protein isoforms, notably ∆133p53β are expressed at higher levels in MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Depletion of Δ133 or β p53 variants significantly decreased the invasiveness of mutant TP53 MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells without altering the expression of mutant TAp53α protein.
source: Importantly, depletion of Δ133 or β p53 variants (by transfection of si133-1, si133-2 or siβ) significantly decreased the invasiveness of mutant TP53 MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells without altering the expression of mutant TAp53α protein (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay and western blot data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Depletion of all p53 isoforms except Δ133p53 (α, β, γ) by siTA did not change the invasive activity of MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells.
source: However, depletion of all p53 isoforms except Δ133p53 (α, β, γ) by siTA did not change the invasive activity of MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells, indicating that the simultaneous depletion of all TAp53 (including mutant TAp53α) did not impair MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cell invasion (Figures 3B and Figure 3—figures supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data presented in Figures 3B and Figure 3—figures supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of the si133-1- and si133-2- resistant Δ133p53β-R280K rescued invasion in MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells depleted of Δ133p53 isoforms.
source: As expected, expression of the si133-1- and si133-2- resistant Δ133p53β-R280K rescued invasion (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data presented in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Δ133p53β-R280K expression rescued invasion when cells were depleted of all β isoforms by siβ.
source: Similarly, Δ133p53β-R280K expression rescued invasion when cells were depleted of all β isoforms by siβ (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data presented in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: All three mutant Δ133p53 isoforms rescued invasion in cells depleted of ∆133p53 variants, with Δ133p53β-R280K conferring the highest invasive activity compared to Δ133p53α-R280K or Δ133p53γ-R280K.
source: All three mutant Δ133p53 isoforms rescued invasion in cells depleted of ∆133p53 variants, with Δ133p53β-R280K conferring the highest invasive activity compared to Δ133p53α-R280K or Δ133p53γ-R280K (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data presented in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depletion of mutant Δ133 or β p53 isoforms reversed mesenchymal traits of MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells, by inducing a significant induction of E-Cadherin protein expression and a marked decrease in Vimentin expression.
source: Interestingly, depletion of mutant Δ133 or β p53 isoforms reversed mesenchymal traits of MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells, by inducing a significant induction of E-Cadherin protein expression and a marked decrease in Vimentin expression, particularly in cells transfected with siβ.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Re-epithelialization was impaired upon depletion of all p53 isoforms.
source: Interestingly, re-epithelialization was impaired upon depletion of all p53 isoforms (Figure 3D, lane siE7), suggesting that other p53 splice variants control epithelial features.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 3D and leads to an inference about the role of other p53 variants.

claim: WT Δ133p53β triggered MCF7 cell invasion into type1-Collagen.
source: As shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, WT Δ133p53β triggered MCF7 cell invasion into type1-Collagen.
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data presented in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Metastasis-derived cell lines expressing WT or mutant TP53 exhibited a higher ability to invade Matrigel compared to cells derived from primary colon tumors.
source: Compared to cells derived from primary colon tumors, metastasis-derived cell lines expressing WT or mutant TP53 exhibited a higher ability to invade Matrigel (Figure 4A) and had no E-Cadherin at cell-cell junctions (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay and immunofluorescence data presented in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Metastasis-derived cell lines had no E-Cadherin at cell-cell junctions.
source: Compared to cells derived from primary colon tumors, metastasis-derived cell lines expressing WT or mutant TP53 exhibited a higher ability to invade Matrigel (Figure 4A) and had no E-Cadherin at cell-cell junctions (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Δ133p53 mRNA expression was significantly higher in the invasive cell lines whether they express WT or mutant TP53 gene, i.e. LoVo, SW620 and CoLo205, as compared with HCT116 and SW480 cell lines.
source: We thus measured Δ133p53 mRNA expression by RT-qPCR (Taqman) and found it significantly higher in the invasive cell lines whether they express WT or mutant TP53 gene, i.e. LoVo, SW620 and CoLo205, as compared with HCT116 and SW480 cell lines (Figure 4C), in agreement with the results obtained in the breast cancer cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Knockdown of Δ133p53 isoforms in mutant TP53 SW620, or WT TP53 LoVo CRC cells led to a significant decrease in invasive capacity in both cell lines.
source: To confirm the role of Δ133p53 isoforms in cell invasion, we knocked-down these isoforms in mutant TP53 SW620, or WT TP53 LoVo CRC cells by using si133-1 and si133-2, which led to a significant decrease invasive capacity in both cell lines (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figures supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data presented in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figures supplement 1A and B.

claim: Re-introduction of si133-1-resistant WT Δ133p53β rescued invasiveness of LoVo cells depleted of Δ133p53 isoforms by si133-1.
source: As expected, re-introduction of si133-1-resistant WT Δ133p53β rescued invasiveness of LoVo cells depleted of Δ133p53 isoforms by si133-1 (Figure 4—figures supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data presented in Figure 4—figures supplement 1C and D.

claim: HCT116 cells transfected with siTAp53 are more invasive than cells transfected with siNS or siE7.
source: HCT116 cells transfected with siTAp53 are more invasive than cells transfected with siNS or siE7, while HCT116 cells transfected with siβ, which depleted p53β, ∆40p53β and ∆133p53β are less invasive than cells transfected with siNS (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data presented in Figures 4E and F.

claim: HCT116 cells transfected with siβ are less invasive than cells transfected with siNS.
source: HCT116 cells transfected with siTAp53 are more invasive than cells transfected with siNS or siE7, while HCT116 cells transfected with siβ, which depleted p53β, ∆40p53β and ∆133p53β are less invasive than cells transfected with siNS (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data presented in Figures 4E and F.

claim: The ratio of TAp53 and β isoforms, including ∆133p53β, defines the invasive activity of HCT116 cells.
source: This suggests that the ratio of TAp53 and β isoforms, including ∆133p53β, defines the invasive activity of HCT116 cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that modulating different p53 isoforms affects HCT116 invasiveness.

claim: GFP-tagged Δ133p53β expression elicited a significant increase of rounded cells with dynamic bleb-like structures on their surface.
source: GFP-tagged Δ133p53β expression elicited a significant increase of rounded cells with dynamic bleb-like structures on their surface (Figure 5A, Video 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A as control).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data presented in Figure 5A and Video 1.

claim: Blebbing cells were alive and were not undergoing apoptosis.
source: Propidium iodide staining and FACS analysis showed that blebbing cells were alive and were not undergoing apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The number of blebbing cells was 25 times greater than the number of adherent cells in HCT116 cells transfected with Δ133p53β.
source: The number of blebbing cells was 25 times greater than the number of adherent cells in HCT116 cells transfected with Δ133p53β (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: E-cadherin and β1-integrin, expressed at high levels in adherent cohesive cells, were barely detected in blebbing cells.
source: As shown in Figure 5C,E-cadherin and β1-integrin, expressed at high levels in adherent cohesive cells, were barely detected in blebbing cells, implying they had experienced EAT.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Δ133p53β expression in HCT116 cells elicited a two-fold increase in migration.
source: Δ133p53β also enhanced cell migration and invasion, since its expression in HCT116 cells elicited a two-fold increase in migration (Figure 5D) in uncoated transwell chambers and conferred a 5 times higher invasive capacity in Matrigel (Figure 5D) compared to GFP-only-transfected controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by migration assay data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Δ133p53β expression in HCT116 cells conferred a 5 times higher invasive capacity in Matrigel compared to GFP-only-transfected controls.
source: Δ133p53β also enhanced cell migration and invasion, since its expression in HCT116 cells elicited a two-fold increase in migration (Figure 5D) in uncoated transwell chambers and conferred a 5 times higher invasive capacity in Matrigel (Figure 5D) compared to GFP-only-transfected controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Knockdown of Δ133p53 isoforms in LoVo cells remarkably decreased 3-D cell scattering.
source: Knockdown of Δ133p53 isoforms in LoVo cells remarkably decreased 3-D cell scattering, a process which shares cellular features reminiscent of cells undergoing EMT/EAT (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3-D cell scattering assay data presented in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: LoVo transduced with control shNS progressively detached and migrated as individual cells.
source: LoVo transduced with control shNS progressively detached and migrated as individual cells (arrows, Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by wound-healing assay data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: LoVo depleted of Δ133p53 isoforms still remain cohesive and migrate very slowly into the gap.
source: LoVo depleted of Δ133p53 isoforms still remain cohesive and migrate very slowly into the gap.
evidence: This claim is supported by wound-healing assay data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Endogenous Δ133p53 protein isoforms regulate both the mode of cell motility and the ability to implement adherens junctions, with a subsequent impact on cell velocity.
source: Thus endogenous Δ133p53 protein isoforms regulate both the mode of cell motility and the ability to implement adherens junctions, with a subsequent impact on cell velocity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the wound-healing assay observations.

claim: Δ133p53β expression elicits hallmarks of EAT/EMT in CRC cells.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that Δ133p53β expression elicits hallmarks of EAT/EMT in CRC cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple experimental observations in colon cancer cells.

claim: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in a wide range of cancer types.
source: Recent whole cancer genome sequencing studies have conclusively established that the tumor suppressor gene, TP53, is the most frequently mutated gene in a wide range of cancer types.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from whole cancer genome sequencing studies.

claim: Defects in TP53 tumor suppressor activity are a compulsory step to cancer formation.
source: Altogether these data strongly suggest that defects in TP53 tumor suppressor activity are a compulsory step to cancer formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental and clinical data about TP53's role in cancer.

claim: TP53 gene, whether WT or mutant, has a paramount biological and clinical role in response to cancer treatment.
source: In addition, ample data have also demonstrated that TP53 gene, whether WT or mutant, has a paramount biological and clinical role in response to cancer treatment (Brosh and Rotter, 2009; Do et al., 2012; Jackson et al., 2012; Muller et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: The three mRNAs (Δ133p53α, Δ133p53β, Δ133p53γ) are initiated from the same promoter in intron-4 of the human TP53 gene.
source: The strong association of Δ133p53α with either the Δ133p53β or Δ133p53γ isoforms is consistent with the fact that the three mRNAs are initiated from the same promoter in intron-4 of the human TP53 gene (Bourdon et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Δ133p53α, Δ133p53β, and Δ133p53γ are not randomly expressed in breast cancers.
source: This indicates that Δ133p53 (α, β, γ) isoforms are not randomly expressed in breast cancers, confirming that the internal promoter of TP53 and the alternative (β, γ) splicing of p53 mRNA are regulated in tumor cells (Aoubala et al., 2011; Marcel et al., 2014; 2010; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the expression patterns observed in breast tumors, supported by citations.

claim: Detection of Δ133p53β at time of surgery in primary luminal-A breast tumors of patients devoid of lymph node would predict cancer progression.
source: It implies that at the time of surgery, detection of Δ133p53β in primary luminal-A breast tumors of patients devoid of lymph node would predict cancer progression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the multivariate analysis showing Δ133p53β as an independent predictor of cancer recurrence.

claim: WT TP53 gene would promote breast cancer recurrence and increased risk of death when it expresses Δ133p53β.
source: Therefore, far from having its function inactivated in Luminal A breast cancer, the WT TP53 gene would promote breast cancer recurrence and increased risk of death when it expresses Δ133p53β.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clinical data showing Δ133p53β association with poor outcomes in luminal-A breast cancer.

claim: The invasive activity of MCF7, MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells is positively correlated to the Δ133p53 mRNA expression level.
source: First, we observed that the invasive activity of MCF7, MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells is positively correlated to the Δ133p53 mRNA expression level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing invasion assays with RT-qPCR data.

claim: The expression of mutant TAp53α is not sufficient to explain why the triple negative breast cancer MDA-MB-231 and its highly metastatic MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN derived clone have different invasive activity.
source: However, expression of the mutant TAp53α is not sufficient to explain why the triple negative breast cancer MDA-MB-231 and its highly metastatic MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN derived clone have different invasive activity while they both express the same mutant TP53-R280K gene.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that both cell lines express the same mutant TP53 but have different invasiveness.

claim: The role of endogenous mutant Δ133p53 isoforms in promoting invasiveness may be extended to other tissue types.
source: This indicates that the role of endogenous mutant Δ133p53 isoforms in promoting invasiveness may be extended to other tissue types and that endogenous Δ133p53 isoform expression regulates cancer cell invasion in TP53 mutant colon and breast cancer cells, irrespective of the full-length p53 (TAp53α) expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations in both breast and colon cancer cell lines.

claim: Endogenous Δ133p53 isoform expression regulates cancer cell invasion in TP53 mutant colon and breast cancer cells, irrespective of the full-length p53 (TAp53α) expression.
source: This indicates that the role of endogenous mutant Δ133p53 isoforms in promoting invasiveness may be extended to other tissue types and that endogenous Δ133p53 isoform expression regulates cancer cell invasion in TP53 mutant colon and breast cancer cells, irrespective of the full-length p53 (TAp53α) expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data showing Δ133p53 effects independent of TAp53α levels.

claim: ∆133p53 isoform expression explains the inconsistent clinical association between TP53 mutation and metastasis.
source: ∆133p53 isoform expression thus explains the inconsistent clinical association between TP53 mutation and metastasis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Δ133p53 promotes invasion regardless of TP53 mutation status.

claim: Epigenetic mechanisms that stem Δ133p53β expression, i.e. alternative splicing and induction of the TP53 internal promoter favour cancer invasion and dissemination of metastatic cells, regardless of TP53 mutation status.
source: These data suggest that epigenetic mechanisms that stem Δ133p53β expression, i.e. alternative splicing and induction of the TP53 internal promoter favour cancer invasion and dissemination of metastatic cells, regardless of TP53 mutation status.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing Δ133p53β promotes invasion in both WT and mutant TP53 cells.

claim: ∆133p53α stimulates angiogenesis and cell invasion.
source: This is in accordance with recent reports showing that ∆133p53α stimulate angiogenesis and cell invasion (Bernard et al., 2013; Roth et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent published studies.

claim: The ∆133p53β isoform is the most efficient promoter of invasion.
source: Here we identified the ∆133p53β isoform as being the most efficient promoter of invasion, corroborating its role as a predictive indicator of cancer relapse and death in the clinic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data comparing the three Δ133p53 isoforms and clinical data.

claim: Expression of Δ133p53β promotes acquisition of a rounded-blebbing movement, which is associated with decrease of E-cadherin and β1-integrin in colon cancer HCT116 cells.
source: Our data indicate that expression of Δ133p53β promotes acquisition of a rounded-blebbing movement, which is associated with decrease of E-cadherin and β1-integrin in colon cancer HCT116 cells.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental observations from microscopy and western blot data.

claim: Δ133p53β (whether WT or mutant) plays a critical role in the induction of cell invasion and EMT/EAT.
source: Our study supports a critical role for Δ133p53β (whether WT or mutant) in the induction of cell invasion and EMT/EAT.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: The biological activities associated with WT or mutant TP53 gene expression are not carried out by the single full-length p53 protein (TAp53α).
source: In summary, our data lead us to conclude that the biological activities associated with WT or mutant TP53 gene expression are not carried out by the single full-length p53 protein (TAp53α).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing p53 isoforms have distinct roles.

claim: p53 isoforms underlie the dual role of WT TP53 gene in preventing or promoting cancer cell invasion.
source: p53 isoforms underlie the dual role of WT TP53 gene in preventing or promoting cancer cell invasion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and clinical data showing different p53 isoforms have opposing effects on invasion.

claim: The invasive activities of cancer cells expressing WT or mutant TP53 gene can be enhanced or inhibited by respectively increasing or reducing expression of Δ133p53β.
source: The invasive activities of cancer cells expressing WT or mutant TP53 gene can be enhanced or inhibited by respectively increasing or reducing expression of Δ133p53β (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental observations from gain- and loss-of-function studies.

claim: Testing the prognostic discriminatory potential of Δ133p53β could influence clinical practice and may offer appropriate and yet unexplored therapeutic options for mutant or WT TP53 tumors expressing Δ133p53β.
source: Testing the prognostic discriminatory potential of Δ133p53β could influence clinical practice and may offer appropriate and yet unexplored therapeutic options for mutant or WT TP53 tumors expressing Δ133p53β.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications based on the study findings.

claim: Mutant TAp53α protein can activate cell migration, invasion and metastasis.
source: The difference between MCF7 cells and the two MDA-MB-231 cell lines may result from their TP53 status, since mutant TAp53α protein can activate cell migration, invasion and metastasis (Gadea et al., 2007, 2002; Muller et al., 2009; Roger et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Overexpression of mutant TAp53α promotes integrin and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) recycling, thus driving invasion.
source: It has previously been reported that overexpression of mutant TAp53α promotes integrin and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) recycling, thus driving invasion (Muller et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: SW480 and SW620 cells express the same mutant TP53-R273H gene.
source: Although SW480 and SW620 cells express the same mutant TP53-R273H gene, SW480 cells are far less invasive than the SW620 cells.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the genetic status of these cell lines.

claim: SW480 cells are far less invasive than the SW620 cells.
source: Although SW480 and SW620 cells express the same mutant TP53-R273H gene, SW480 cells are far less invasive than the SW620 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: SW480 cells express much less Δ133p53 mRNAs than the SW620 cells.
source: Interestingly, SW480 cells express much less Δ133p53 mRNAs than the SW620 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Depletion of endogenous Δ133p53 isoforms from SW620 cells reduces cell invasion, despite unaltered and strong expression of mutant TAp53α protein.
source: Importantly, depletion of endogenous Δ133p53 isoforms from SW620 cells reduces cell invasion, despite unaltered and strong expression of mutant TAp53α protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay and western blot data.

claim: Depletion of ∆133p53 isoforms in WT TP53 colon carcinoma LoVo cells abolishes their scattering and invasive activities.
source: Importantly, the invasive activity of Δ133p53 isoforms is not associated with TP53 mutation status since depletion of ∆133p53 isoforms in WT TP53 colon carcinoma LoVo cells abolishes their scattering and invasive activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3-D cell scattering and invasion assay data.

claim: The invasive activity of Δ133p53 isoforms is not associated with TP53 mutation status.
source: Importantly, the invasive activity of Δ133p53 isoforms is not associated with TP53 mutation status since depletion of ∆133p53 isoforms in WT TP53 colon carcinoma LoVo cells abolishes their scattering and invasive activities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations in both WT and mutant TP53 cell lines.

claim: The introduction of WT Δ133p53β in the poorly invasive WT TP53 MCF7 breast cancer cells that express all WT p53 isoforms but Δ133p53β, enhances MCF7 invasive activity.
source: Interestingly, the introduction of WT Δ133p53β in the poorly invasive WT TP53 MCF7 breast cancer cells that express all WT p53 isoforms but Δ133p53β, enhances MCF7 invasive activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data.

claim: HCT116 invasive activity is inhibited after depletion of Δ133p53 or β isoforms by siRNA si133 or siβ respectively.
source: Hence HCT116 invasive activity is inhibited after depletion of Δ133p53 or β isoforms by siRNA si133 or siβ respectively while HCT116 invasive activity is enhanced after depletion of WT full-length p53 proteins (TAp53α, TAp53β, TAp53γ, Δ40p53α, Δ40p53β and Δ40p53γ) by siRNA siTA.
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data.

claim: HCT116 invasive activity is enhanced after depletion of WT full-length p53 proteins (TAp53α, TAp53β, TAp53γ, Δ40p53α, Δ40p53β and Δ40p53γ) by siRNA siTA.
source: Hence HCT116 invasive activity is inhibited after depletion of Δ133p53 or β isoforms by siRNA si133 or siβ respectively while HCT116 invasive activity is enhanced after depletion of WT full-length p53 proteins (TAp53α, TAp53β, TAp53γ, Δ40p53α, Δ40p53β and Δ40p53γ) by siRNA siTA.
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data.

claim: Ectopic expression of WT Δ133p53β in HCT116 cells enhances their invasive activity.
source: Furthermore, ectopic expression of WT Δ133p53β in HCT116 cells enhances their invasive activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by invasion assay data.

claim: Δ133p53β expression provides a rationale for invasive cancers expressing WT TP53 and non-invasive cancers expressing missense mutant TP53.
source: Altogether, Δ133p53β expression provides a rationale for invasive cancers expressing WT TP53 and non-invasive cancers expressing missense mutant TP53.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and clinical data.

claim: The invasive capacity of colon cancer cell lines correlates with and depends on the expression of Δ133p53 isoforms, regardless of the TP53 mutation status.
source: Altogether our data indicate that the invasive capacity of colon cancer cell lines, as in the breast tumor cell lines, correlates with and depends on the expression of Δ133p53 isoforms, regardless of the TP53 mutation status.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from experimental data in colon cancer cell lines.

claim: Mutant Δ133p53 isoforms, notably the Δ133p53β variant, are sufficient to promote invasion in mutant TP53 MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells.
source: These results indicate that mutant Δ133p53 isoforms, notably the Δ133p53β variant, are sufficient to promote invasion in mutant TP53 MDA-MB-231 D3H2LN cells, consistently with an active role for Δ133p53β isoform in cancer progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiment data.

claim: Δ133p53 isoforms, notably Δ133p53β, regulate invasion, irrespectively of TP53 mutation status.
source: This indicates that Δ133p53 isoforms, notably Δ133p53β, regulate invasion, irrespectively of TP53 mutation status.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data in both WT and mutant TP53 colon cancer cells.

claim: Cell invasiveness is regulated by Δ133p53β irrespective of whether they harbor a mutant or a WT p53 gene.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that cell invasiveness is regulated by Δ133p53β irrespective of whether they harbor a mutant or a WT p53 gene.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from experimental data in multiple cell lines.

claim: The WT TP53 gene can also promote invasiveness by encoding Δ133p53β.
source: Challenging the paradigm that WT TP53 always acts as a tumor suppressor protein, our data show that the WT TP53 gene can also promote invasiveness by encoding Δ133p53β.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental and clinical data showing WT Δ133p53β promotes invasion.

claim: The cell decision is not exclusively determined by canonical full-length p53 protein (TAp53α), either mutant or WT, but by the modular protein complex of p53 isoforms.
source: Hence, our data established that the cell decision is not exclusively determined by canonical full- length p53 protein (TAp53α), either mutant or WT, but by the modular protein complex of p53 isoforms, which reprogram epithelial cells to pro-metastatic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing p53 isoforms have distinct and important roles.

claim: The modular protein complex of p53 isoforms reprogram epithelial cells to pro-metastatic cells.
source: Hence, our data established that the cell decision is not exclusively determined by canonical full- length p53 protein (TAp53α), either mutant or WT, but by the modular protein complex of p53 isoforms, which reprogram epithelial cells to pro-metastatic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing p53 isoforms promote EMT/EAT.

claim: Δ133p53β increases risk of cancer recurrence and death in breast cancer patients.
source: Δ133p53β increases risk of cancer recurrence and death in breast cancer patients.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by clinical data analysis.

claim: Δ133p53β is critical to define invasiveness in a panel of breast and colon cell lines, expressing WT or mutant TP53.
source: Furthermore Δ133p53β is critical to define invasiveness in a panel of breast and colon cell lines, expressing WT or mutant TP53.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in multiple cell lines.

claim: Endogenous mutant Δ133p53β depletion prevents invasiveness without affecting mutant full-length p53 protein expression.
source: Endogenous mutant Δ133p53β depletion prevents invasiveness without affecting mutant full-length p53 protein expression.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: WT and mutant Δ133p53β induces EMT.
source: Mechanistically WT and mutant Δ133p53β induces EMT.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing EMT markers.

claim: WT TP53 can promote cancer cell invasion.
source: Our findings provide explanations to 2 long-lasting and important clinical conundrums: how WT TP53 can promote cancer cell invasion and reciprocally why mutant TP53 gene does not systematically induce cancer progression.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental and clinical data.

claim: Mutant TP53 gene does not systematically induce cancer progression.
source: Our findings provide explanations to 2 long-lasting and important clinical conundrums: how WT TP53 can promote cancer cell invasion and reciprocally why mutant TP53 gene does not systematically induce cancer progression.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental and clinical data.
